Introduction Sulfur is a promising cathode material for the next-generation energy storage batteries due to its high theoretical capacity of 1675 mAh g−1.[1] When coupled with lithium metal anode (theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh g−1), theoretical capacity Conventional lithium–sulfur batteries often suffer from fatal problems such as high flammability, polysulfide shuttling, and lithium dendrites growth.

Here, highly-safe lithium–sulfur batteries based on flame-retardant electrolyte (dimethoxyether/1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether) coupled with functional separator (nanoconductive carbon-coated cellulose nonwoven) to resolve aforementioned bottle-neck issues are demonstrated.
It is found that this flame-retardant electrolyte exhibits excellent flame retardancy and low solubility of polysulfide.

In addition, Li/Li symmetrical cells using such flame-retardant electrolyte deliver extraordinary longterm cycling stability (less than 10 mV overpotential) for over 2500 h at 1.0 mA cm−2 and 1.0 mAh cm−2.

Moreover, bare sulfur cathode–based lithium–sulfur batteries using this flame retardant electrolyte coupled with nanoconductive carbon-coated cellulose separator can retain 83.6% discharge capacity after 200 cycles at 0.5 C.
Under high charge/discharge rate (4 C), lithium–sulfur cells still show high charge/discharge capacity of ≈350 mAh g−1.
Even at an elevated temperature of 60 °C, discharge capacity of 870 mAh g−1 can be retained.
More importantly, high-loading bare sulfur cathode (4 mg cm−2)–based lithium–sulfur batteries can also deliver high charge/discharge capacity over 806 mAh g−1 after 56 cycles.

Undoubtedly, the strategy of flame retardant electrolyte coupled with carbon-coated separator enlightens highly safe lithium–sulfur batteries at a wide range of temperature. of lithium-batteries can reach up to 2600 Wh kg−1, which is much higher than that of conventional lithium ion batteries.[2] Unfortunately, there are still several problems need to be solved.

For the cathode side, polysulfide can dissolve into ether-based electrolyte and then shuttling to anode side, reacting with lithium metal anode and eventually leading to irreversible capacity fading and low Coulombic efficiency (CE).[3] For the lithium metal anode side, uneven Li+ platting/ stripping easily leads to the rapid growth of lithium dendrites, which can easily penetrate separator and causing internal short circuit.

Lithium dendrites and fragile electrolyte/electrode interface could detach from lithium metal anode to form “dead Li,” more electrolyte would be consumed and the lithium utilization is reduced.[4] For electrolyte, conventional ether-based electrolytes are easily volatile and highly flammable,[5] which is detrimental for safety of lithium–sulfur batteries.
Great efforts have been carried out to solve the issues associated with lithium– sulfur batteries noted above.
To address the problem of lithium polysulfide shuttling, various strategies have been explored, including using modified structure sulfur host[6] and using ionic liquid electrolyte,[7] etc.

To find out the solution to a dendrite free lithium metal anode, researchers have done many attempts such as design special architecture lithium metal anode,[8] pre-formed solid electrolyte interface,[9] modified separators[10] and etc.
Generally speaking, these methods usually only solve the problems of the cathode or anode unilaterally.

To restrain the dendrite growth and prevent polysulfide shuttling simultaneously, most of the researches focused on the solid or quasi-solid state electrolyte.[6f] Armand et al.[11] studied solid state polymer electrolytes (SPEs) using poly (ethylene oxide) (PEO) as polymer matrix, lithium–sulfur batteries using PEO-based SPE exhibits high specific discharge capacity of 1395 mAh g−1.

He et al.[12] developed solid state lithium–sulfur batteries using Li1.5Al0.5Ge1.5(PO4)3 (LAGP) as the electrolyte, under the elevated temperature of 55 °C and the current density of 20 mA g−1, a capacity of 1524 mAh g−1 could be obtained.

What’s more, the active mass loading usually cannot meet the demand of practical application.
Therefore, there is still a long way to go before all-solid state lithium– sulfur batteries application.

Flame retardant electrolyte has attracted wide interest as a new research hotspot, Wang et al.[13] added tris(2,2,2-trifluoroethyl) phosphite as the flame retardant additive into the conventional carbonate electrolyte to obtain the flame inhibiting electrolyte, which enables the sulfur@PAN composite cathode lithium–sulfur battery superior long cycle stability and rate performance (800 mAh g−1 at 10 C).
However, this flame inhibiting electrolyte could still caught fire even though the electrolyte could be self-extinguished after several seconds.

Continues study was carried on and they proposed an intrinsic flame retardant electrolyte using flame-retardant triethyl phosphate and high flashpoint 1H,1H,5H-octafluoropentyl-1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (TTE) as cosolvent,[14] the lithium–sulfur batteries delivers high discharge capacity and stable cycle performance.

Hexafluorocyclotriphosphazene as a kind of flame retardant additive was introduced into conventional 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)/dimethoxyether (DME) electrolyte for lithium–sulfur batteries,[15] but the cycle performance is not stable enough.

Recently, Wang et al.[16] reported a kind of localized high concentration electrolyte composed by the inert fluoroalkyl ether of TTE and highly concentrated lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl) imide/DME, the high flash point and inert nature of the fluoroalkyl ether makes the electrolyte hard to be ignited.
The discharge capacity of 775 mAh g−1 was obtained, but the rate performance and cathode sulfur loading needs to be further improved.

These excellent works on the flame retardant electrolyte of lithium–sulfur batteries still have some unsatisfactory aspects, current researches are mainly focused on S@PAN and S@C composite cathode, their moderate sulfur content and energy-consuming preparation process in the inert atmosphere at high temperature hinders the commercialization of lithium–sulfur batteries.

Herein, we proposed a strategy of inflammable electrolyte combined with nanoconductive carbon-coated separators to improve the overall performance of bare sulfur cathode–based lithium–sulfur batteries.

The as-prepared inflammable electrolyte was composed by simply mixing 2 m LiTFSI/DME with TTE in the volume ratio of 1:4 (denoted as TDE, the average LiTFSI concentration is about 0.4 m), it possess both properties of reducing polysulfide shuttling and stabilizing the lithium metal, the inflammable nature of TTE can remarkably improve the safety of lithium–sulfur batteries. the TDE electrolyte coupled with nanoconductive carbon-coated separator (denote as CS separator) enables the bare sulfur cathode–based batteries excellent rate performance of ≈350 mAh g−1 at 4 C, the initial discharge capacity could reach up to 1187 mAh g−1 at the cathode sulfur loading of 4 mg cm−2 (equals to the areal capacity of 6.7 mAh g−1).
What is more, the batteries using TDE electrolyte could maintain a stable cycle performance at high temperature (60 °C).
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work of flame retardant electrolyte reported for the high areal capacity bare sulfur cathode–based lithium–sulfur battery so far. 2.
Results and Discussion 2.1.

Physical and Chemical Properties TDE electrolyte was prepared by simply mixing 2 m LiTFSI/ DME (with 0.1 m LiNO3, all of the following mentioned contain the same amount) with TTE in different volume ratio.
Due to the good compatibility of TTE and DME, the as prepared TDE electrolyte shows a uniform and transparent characteristic (Figure 1a).

According to the flame retardant test shows in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), when the volume ratio of TTE in the mixture solvent is higher than 80% (TTE:2 m LiTFSI/DME = 4:1), spray formed by the TDE electrolyte can effectively extinguish the burning paper roll, however, with the volume ratio of inert TTE increasing, the ionic conductivity is decreasing, thus the volume ratio of TTE: 2 m LiTFSI/ DME = 4:1 is chosen for the flame retardant TDE electrolyte (the concentration of LiNO3 in the TDE electrolyte is around 0.025 m).

As shown in Figure 1b, TDE electrolyte exhibits the viscosity of 1.091 mPa s, lower than pristine 2 m LiTFSI/DME and conventional electrolyte (1 m LiTFSI DOL/DME with 1 wt% LiNO3, denoted as LS002 in the following section).
Raman spectroscopy (Figure 1c) was used to investigate the solvate structure and the coordination between Li+ and solvent.

With the increasing of LiTFSI concentration in DME, the peak of COC located around 820–830 cm−1 is weakened, peak intensity of interaction between Li+ and O atom at around 870–880 cm−1 is growing, indicating the interaction between Li+ and O atom is getting stronger.

However, no matter what concentration of DME is mixed with TTE in volume ration of 1:4, the COC peak of TTE around 830–840 cm−1 is hardly changed in intensity and location, demonstrated that the TTE molecular barely binds with Li+.
As can be seen from Figure S2 (Supporting Information), the band at 1246.7 cm−1 is attributed to aggregated LiTFSI, the band at 1243.1 cm−1 is attributed to free TFSI−.
Both 1 m LiTFSI/DME and 2 m LiTFSI/DME shows the same TFSI− Raman shift at 1243.1 cm−1, which means the solvate structure of 1 m and 2 m LiTFSI/DME is the same.

After blended 2 m LiTFSI/DME with TTE in the volume ratio of 1:4 to get TDE electrolyte, the band of TFSI- shifts towards higher wave number at 1244.8 cm−1, this is very close to the TFSI− peak position of 5 m LiTFSI/DME, which means the contact ion pair is formed.
The above experimental results show that after blend 2 m LiTFSI/DME with TTE, the interaction between DME, Li+, and TFSI− is enhanced (Figure 1d).

The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) plots of Stainless steel/Stainless steel cells using TDE, LS002 electrolyte, and 2 m LiTFSI/DME electrolyte at room temperature is presented in Figure 2a, ionic conductivity of TDE (0.990 mS cm−1) is slightly lower than that of the other two comparisons, and this can be attributed to the lower salt concentration (0.4 m LiTFSI with 0.025 m LiNO3) in the TDE electrolyte.

Figure 2b shows the electrochemical stability window of the 2 m LiTFSI DME, LS002 electrolyte, and TDE electrolyte, the decomposition voltage of TDE electrolyte starts at 4.7 V versus Li/Li+, and it is stable enough for the lithium–sulfur battery.
Lithium transfer number (tLi+) of TDE electrolyte is around 0.4842.

Interfacial Stability To demonstrate the TDE electrolyte can effectively stabilize the Li metal anode/electrolyte interfaces, symmetric Li/Li cells using LS002 and TDE electrolyte were assembled respectively.

Under the high current density of 2.5 mA cm−2 to a 5 mAh cm−2 capacity (Figure 3a), the Li/Li cells using LS002 electrolyte shows the overpotential of over 50 mV (Figure 3b), as reference, Li/Li cells using LS002 electrolyte shows a stable time-voltage profile with overpotential of 30 mV (Figure 3c).

Both TDE and LS002 electrolyte steadily cycled over 2500 h at the current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 to a 1.0 mAh cm−2 capacity (Figure 3d), the overpotential of TDE electrolyte–based Li/Li symmetric cell is always less than the LS002 electrolyte–based Li/Li symmetric cell (insert plot in Figure 3d), which indicated the lower interface impedance of TDE electrolyte/electrode interface.

To further demonstrate the stability of TDE electrolyte during the Li stripping/plating process, the Li/Cu half cells were assembled and cycled at the current density of 0.1 mA cm−2 to a capacity of 0.1 mAh cm−2 using TDE and LS002 electrolyte respectively.

Conversely, the fluctuate CE value of Li/Cu cells with the LS002 electrolyte sharply declined during the charge/discharge process, such poor performance confirms the unstable reductive stability of LS002 electrolyte to Li metal anode.

Figures S4 and S5 (Supporting Information) show the overpotential for Li stripping and plating in the Li/Cu cells using TDE electrolyte, the voltage polarization of Li/Cu cells using TDE electrolyte continues to decrease during cycling (from 1.0621 V at the first cycle to 0.0406 V at the 40th cycle), this can be attributed to the improvement of the electrode/electrolyte interface during the cycling, besides, the low overpotential indicates fast plating/ stripping kinetics of Li+ in the TDE electrolyte.[17] Obviously, the excellent cycle stability and limited overpotential of Li/Li cells and Li/Cu cells using TDE electrolyte indicates that the TDE helps stabilize the electrode/electrolyte interface. 2.3.

Interface Characterization Lithium metal was peeled off from Li/Li symmetric cells after 100 h cycles at the current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 and 1.0 mAh cm−2, the morphology of lithium metal surface and cross section (Figure 3e–h) is tested by scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

Li metal electrode from Li/Li symmetric cells using the LS002 electrolyte shows a porous and fragmented surface (Figure 3e), the specific area of Li metal surface was enlarged thus more interfacial reactions would be introduced and causing unstable SEI interface and continuous electrolyte consumption.
The rough and easily peeled surface is easy to loss electrical connection with Li metal electrode and then bring about dead Li, which eventually leading to battery failure.

On the contrary, the deposited Li film from Li/Li symmetric cells using TDE electrolyte shows dendrites free surface (Figure 3g), besides, it can be seen from the cross section (Figure 3f,h) that the lithium electrode from Li/Li cells using TDE electrolyte has a denser deposit Li layer.
The deposited Li layer is flexible enough even if the lithium electrode is distorted during cutting with a scalpel, the deposited Li layer is still firmly attached to the Li electrode.

To further reveal the unique surface properties in TDE electrolyte, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and time-offlight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) analysis was employed to reveal the component and the component’s distribution of the SEI layer from Li/Li symmetric cells using different electrolytes.

As can be seen from Figure 4a–f, the CC/CH, CF3, LiF, Li2CO3, Li2O, and organic OCO peaks appear on the surface of Li electrode from the symmetric cells using TDE electrolyte, those chemical components is possibly generated from two ways: 1) reaction with air before sample transfer into XPS vacuum chamber, the Li2CO3 and Li2O could be generated; 2) residual of LiTFSI (CF3) and decomposition of TDE electrolyte (LiF, Li2O, and Li2CO3).

The huge surface energy of LiF makes it harder to get brittle fractured and the relatively smaller lattice constant allows easy plastic deformation,[18] the organic OCO component helps SEI more resilient, thus the soft and rigid LiF-rich SEI film generated by the TDE electrolyte decomposition can suppress the morphological instabilities, which is consistent well with SEM results.
Li2CO3 and Li2O possess higher ionic conductivity (at around 10−8 S cm−1),[19] and is helpful to reduce the interfacial resistance.

Accordingly, the interface created by the TDE electrolyte on the surface of the lithium electrode has some unique properties such as dendrite free, high flexibility, fast ionic migration and endows the enhanced battery safety while avoiding the generation of dead Li and decreasing interfacial resistance.

To further reveal the dendrite free character of TDE electrolyte, in situ electrochemical optical microscope was employed to monitor the surface morphology change of Li electrode in the Li/Li cells during the Li+ platting/stripping process.
All the cells were charged and discharged in the current density of 2 mA cm−2 to the deposit capacity of 2 mAh cm−2.

As can be seen in Figure 5a–d, significant lithium dendrite growth can be found in LS002 electrolyte (Figure 5b), in contrast, dense and flat deposit Li film (Figure 5d) is observed in the TDE electrolyte Li/Li symmetric cells.

The dendrite free character of TDE electrolyte greatly avoid the risks of internal short circuit thus the battery safety is further enhanced, the densely deposited Li layer helps mitigates the formation of dead Li, the long-term cycling stability of lithium metal anode is greatly improved.

Fluorescence Probing Technique was carried out to further figure out the distribution of active Li and detect the accumulation of byproducts on the lithium metal surface from the Li/Li cells using TDE and LS002 electrolyte respectively.
All the Li/Li cells were cycled for 50 cycles under the current density of 1 mA cm−2 to the areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2.

As shown in Figure 5f, lithium metal anode cycled in the LS002 electrolyte exhibit a bright and nonuniform fluorescence distribute, indicating the uneven plating/stripping process of Li+ in the LS002 electrolyte led to the accumulation of byproducts.

On the contrary, as shown in Figure 5h, the fluorescence of lithium metal anode cycled in the TDE electrolyte was nearly undetectable, suggesting an uniformly distributed active Li, the active Li dominated lithium metal surface can effectively lower the interface resistance, which is well consistent with the small overpotential of Li/Li symmetric cells. 2.4.

Li–S Battery Performance Li/S cells with bare sulfur cathode using TDE and LS002 electrolyte were assembled respectively (sulfur loading of ≈1.2 mg cm−2, equals to areal capacity at around 2 mAh cm−2), as shown in Figure 6a, all the batteries were charged/discharged at 0.5 C (equals to current density at around 1 mA cm−2).

TDE electrolyte can effectively reduce polysulfide shuttling, but there are still small amount of polysulfide could be dissolved in the electrolyte according to the UV–vis results of transparent cells mentioned above.

The lower solvation ability to the polysulfide could lower the utilization of sulfur,[21] thus the bare sulfur cathode–based Li/S batteries using TDE electrolyte shows relatively lower discharge capacity (≈200 mAh g−1 at 0.5 C) than LS002 electrolyte.
But it also brought some positive effects, the cycling stability of TDE electrolyte–based Li/S batteries is improved, the discharge capacity keeps almost unchanged over 900 cycles.

Nanoconductive carbon-layer-coated separator (denoted as CS) could further suppress the polysulfide shuttling, furthermore, nanoconductive carbon layer could act as the polysulfide scavenger by provide more redox reaction sites,[22] thus, the utilization of sulfur can be improved.
To fully improve the battery’s cycle stability and performance, CS separator with the coating layer thickness of 10 um were utilized in Li/S batteries (Figure S6, Supporting Information).

As shown in Figure 6a, batteries using TDE electrolyte coupled with CS separator showed much higher discharge capacity (first discharge capacity 903 mAh g−1 at 0.5 C) than cells using TDE electrolyte alone.
This could be attributed to the faster reaction kinetics of polysulfide with the help of CS separator.

Accelerated conversion of soluble high order polysulfide to insoluble low order polysulfide avoids the TDE electrolyte gets saturated, the continuous solvation ability of TDE electrolyte towards polysulfide improves the utilization of sulfur.
When coupled with CS separator, batteries using LS002 electrolyte showed slightly higher discharge capacity than batteries using TDE electrolyte during the first 200 cycles.
This is because higher amount of polysulfide dissolved into LS002 electrolyte and captured by nanoconductive carbon coating, thus the sulfur utilization is significantly improved in a short term.
However, after around 200 cycling, the leading edge of the LS002 electrolyte disappeared.
In the subsequent cycles, cells using TDE electrolyte shows higher discharge capacity and more stable cycle performance.

After 1000 cycles, batteries using TDE electrolyte coupled with CS separator shows 49.4% capacity retention, on the contrary, batteries using LS002 electrolyte coupled with CS separator is only 23.7% of the initial capacity remaining.

Large amount of polysulfide dissolved out from cathode in cells using LS002 electrolyte, excess polysulfide can still pass through the nanoconductive carbon coating layer to reach the lithium metal anode, leading to the fast capacity fading.
The TDE electrolyte has a weaker ability to dissolve polysulfide, and the polysulfide shuttle is further inhibited with the help of the carbon coating layer on the cathode side of the separator.
What’s more, TDE electrolyte helps the lithium metal anode forming a dendritefree interface, thus the cells using TDE electrolyte is more stable than cells using LS002 electrolyte (Figure 7).

Self-discharge, which is a key roadblock for the lithium– sulfur batteries, is caused by the shuttling of the lithium polysulfide.

After several cycles of charge-discharge, the polysulfides dissolved into the electrolyte to form the “catholytes,” during the resting period of lithium–sulfur batteries, the as formed catholytes react with lithium metal anode spontaneously, causing self-discharge and resulting in voltage drop and irreversible capacity loss.[23] Due to the high solubility of LS002 electrolyte to the polysulfide, the severe shuttling effect can cause serious self-discharge, OCV of cells using conventional LS002 electrolyte shows an obvious decay from 2.35 to 2.15 V, which indicates severe capacity loss during resting (Figure S7, Supporting Information).

It is noteworthy that the utilization of TDE electrolyte improves the resistance of self-discharge, after charged to the cutoff voltage of 2.8 V, the cells were resting for 72 hours, during the resting, cells using TDE electrolyte shows stable open cutoff voltage (OCV) at around 2.3 V without obvious decay.
The released self-discharge in the Li–S cells can be ascribed to the reduced polysulfide solubility of TDE electrolyte.

TDE electrolyte/CS separator–based batteries presents superior rate performance (Figure 6d), the capacity maintains 350 mAh g−1 even at the discharge rate of 4 C (equals to current density of 6.7 mA cm−2 at the sulfur loading of 1 mg cm−2).
After 4C charge/discharge, the discharge rate turns back to 0.5 C, and the discharge capacity can still maintains about 900 mAh g−1.
In order to verify the stability of the electrolyte under extreme operating conditions, batteries using TDE and LS002 electrolytes were cycled at 60 °C (Figure 6e).

TDE-CS separator– based batteries electrolyte shows initial discharge capacity of 1557 mAh g−1, close to theoretical capacity, and after 100 cycles the capacity of batteries still remains 870 mAh g−1.
Batteries using LS002 electrolyte coupled with CS separator shows initial discharge capacity of 1671.5 mAh g−1, then the capacity is sharply declined.
The SEM image of Li metal anode in the Li/S cells after 10 cycles at 60 °C is shown in Figure 6f,g, the Li metal anode cycled in LS002 electrolyte exhibits a porous, cracked surface.
On the contrary, lithium metal anode cycled in TDE electrolyte shows a dendrite free interface with only several nodule-like Li deposit.

Under the elevated temperature, conventional electrolytes are more reactive with lithium metal anode, continued consumption of electrolyte and severe shuttle of polysulfide cause a sharp capacity drop in high temperature.
TDE-CS separator–based batteries exhibit excellent stability and discharge capacity at 60 °C, which is due to optimized electrode-electrolyte interface.
TDE electrolyte and CS separator synergistically reduce polysulfides shuttling is also an important contributor.
Excellent high temperature performance allows the battery to withstand extreme conditions, thereby broadening the scope of battery application.
To meet the requirements for practical application, higher areal sulfur mass loading of over 4 mg cm−2 cathode was employed, the long term cycling performance is shown in Figure 6h.

The first discharge capacity of Li/S batteries using TDE electrolyte coupled with CS separator could reach up to 1187 mAh g−1, after 56 cycles, discharge capacity of 806 mAh g−1 remained, CE is higher than 97%.

The initial discharge capacity of Li/S batteries using LS002 electrolyte coupled with CS separator could reach up to 1223.9 mAh g−1, however, the deteriorated anode/electrolyte interface (Figure 6i) lead to low CE value (lowest CE value is at around 80.6%, the highest CE value is at around 93.8%) and rapid capacity decline.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the best performance of flame-retardant electrolyte for high sulfur mass loading bare sulfur cathode– based Li/S cells (Table S1, Supporting Information). 3.
Conclusion In summary, we have developed a multifunctional nonflammable TDE electrolyte that enables dendrite free and stable cycling of lithium metal anode and decrease the shuttle of polysulfide.
The excellent performance of the multifunctional flame-retardant electrolyte can be ascribed to the following points.
First, the lower solubility to the polysulfides hinders the diffusion and shuttling effect, thereby ensuring higher capacity retention (83.6% capacity retention after 200 cycles at 0.5 C).

Second, rigid, flexible SEI film and dendrite free Li metal anode interface is formed during cycling, enables the stable cycling stability of Li/Li cells (cycled over 2500 hours with overpotential of less than 10 mV at current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 and 1.0 mAh cm−2) and Li-Cu cells, the electrolyte/electrode interface is stable enough even at 60 °C (870 mAh g−1 capacity remained after 100 cycles).

Furthermore, after coupled with CS separator, Li/S batteries using TDE electrolyte deliver high initial charge/discharge capacity of 1187 mAh g−1 (CE > 97%) at the cathode sulfur loading of Small 2020, 16, 1905737 Figure 7.

Experimental Section Materials: 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (TTE) (98%) and 9,10-dimethylanthracene were purchased from Energy Chemical Co., Ltd. 1,2-Dimethoxyethane (CP > 99.5%) and lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulphonyl) imide were purchased from Aladdin Co., Ltd. 1.0 m LiTFSI in DOL: DME = 1:1 vol% with 1.0% LiNO3 (LS002) was purchased from DoDoChem.
Preparation Methods—Preparation of TDE Electrolyte: TDE electrolyte was obtained by simply mixing the TTE and 2 m LiTFSI/DME (with 0.1 m LiNO3) electrolyte in 4:1 by volume.

Preparation of Nanoconductive Carbon-Coated Cellulose Nonwoven: the CS-coated separator was prepared by mixing Super P and PVDF binder in mass ratio of 1:1 using N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) as solvent to form a uniform slurry, then the slurry was casting on the cellulose nonwoven using doctor’s blade, then dry at 60 °C in a vacuum oven for 24 h before use.

Preparation of Bare Sulfur Cathode: Bare sulfur cathode was prepared by mixing sulfur, Super P, and PVDF binder in mass ratio of 6:3:1 using NMP as solvent to form the cathode slurry, then the slurry was casting on the aluminum foil by doctor’s blade, then dry at 60 °C in a vacuum oven for 24 h before use.
The sulfur mass loading of ≈1.2 and ≈4 mg cm−2 was prepared in the same way.
All the batteries are tested using LAND CT2001A system in the voltage range of 1.8 V–2.8 V.
Preparation of Li2S6 solution: sublimate sulfur and lithium sulfide were mixed in mole ratio of 5:1, then add in DME solvent and heated at 80 °C for 6 h.
Characterization: The morphology of samples was characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM Hitachi S-4800).
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was carried out using Perkin- Elmer PHI 550 spectrometer equipped with Ar+ sputtering gum using Al Kα source.
Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectroscopy (TOF- SIMS) measurement (IONTOF GmbH, Münster, Germany) with Cs+ sputtering.

Electrochemical Performance—Cyclic Voltammetry: Li/TDE-CS separator/ bare sulfur cathode cells were assembled in the form of CR-2032 type coin cell, the Li metal as the counter electrode and reference electrode, the bare sulfur cathode as the working electrode.
The scan rate was 0.1 mV s−1, and the charge/discharge voltage range was 1.8–2.8 V.

Liner Sweep Voltammetry: Li/electrolyte/stainless steel cells were assembled in the CR-2032 type coin cell, the Li metal as the counter electrode and reference electrode, the stainless steel as the working electrode, the scan rate was 0.1 mV s−1.

Ionic Conductivity Measurement: the ionic conductivity was calculated by the equation of σ = l/SR, the σ is the ionic conductivity, the l is the thickness of separator, S is the electrode area, R is the impedance of electrolyte. the impedance was measured by the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), stainless steel/electrolyte/stainless steel cells were assembled in the CR-2032 type coin cell, the frequency range was from 7 MHz to 100 mHz with the amplitude of 10 mV.

Lithium Transfer Number Measurement: Li/electrolyte/Li cells were assembled in the form of CR-2032 coin cells, the Li+ transfer number (tLi+) of electrolyte was calculated by the Bruce–Vincent–Evans equation: t = Is/I0 × (V − I0R0)/(V – IsRs).
The I0 and Is are obtained via chronoamperometry (CA) under the voltage of 10 mV, R0 and Rs is the initial interface resistance and stable interfacial resistance after the CA process.

To verify the source of SEI component, the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) was calculated (Figure S10a).
It is widely known that lower LUMO suggests the molecular is good electron acceptor, and the higher HOMO suggest the molecular is hard to be oxidized.
The LUMO of DME and TTE is close to each other means they have the same tendency to decompose on the surface of lithium metal.
For further verification, lithium metal was immersed in TTE solvent for 2 hours at ambient temperature.
After 10 s Ar+ etching to remove the surface layer oxidized by air before the lithium metal was moved into the XPS chamber, XPS analysis was carried on to detect the surface component of li metal.
It can be seen from Figure S10 b-d, the C-C/C-H, -CF3, LiF, LiCO3, Li2O, and organic O-C-O peaks appear on the
surface of Li metal surface, almost the same with Li metal anode from the cycled Li/Li cells using TDE electrolyte.
The results of HOMO-LUMO calculation and XPS analysis prove that TTE can participates the SEI formation.

The TDE electrolyte contains tiny amount of LiNO3 additive (0.025M), as is shown in Figure S11 a, the Li/Li cells using LiNO3-free electrolyte shows stable voltage profiles, almost without obvious change during cycling.

For the TDE electrolyte contains tiny amount of LiNO3 (Figure S11 b), the EIS plot of Li/Li symmetric cells was tested at different cycles, as is shown in Figure S11 c-h, it was demonstrated that during the platting/stripping process, the overpotential of Li/Li cells continues to
decrease and finally stabilizes at a certain value.
When the overpotential continues to decrease and stabilizes at around 8 mV, there are still two arcs in the impedance spectrum, thus this couldn’t be internal short-circuit.
The voltage profiles change in the initial cycles can caused by the decomposing of tiny amount of LiNO3 in the TDE electrolyte.

During the initial several cycles, LiNO3 can be reduced to LiNxOy, Li2O species, and fast ion conductor such as Li3N and Li3N derivatives might be generated, thus the impedance of electrolyte/electrode surface can be decreased.
Besides, the decreasing polarization during Li+ platting/stripping of Li-Cu cells using TDE electrolyte (Figure S4, Figure S5) is also a strong proof of the SEI layer generating process.
Previous reports[6] demonstrated that the presence of LiNO3 could remarkably decrease the impedance of Li electrodes, which is well consistent with our results.
